# Results — simulator benchmark

*Generated by `python -m fuelops` on 2026-09-20 (seed 42).
Every number below comes from the disclosed simulator in `fuelops/synthetic_data.py`.
None of it describes a real airline; it describes whether the method holds up.*

**Data:** 24,000 synthetic flights over 24 months.
**Split:** temporal — train 2023-01-01 → 2024-06-29 (18,000 flights, of which the last 20% calibrate the prediction interval), test 2024-06-29 → 2024-12-30 (6,000 flights).

## 1. Model vs baselines (held-out window)

| Model | MAE (kg) | RMSE (kg) | R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean baseline | 238.7 | 294.3 | -0.000 |
| ridge baseline | 97.9 | 135.9 | 0.787 |
| gradient boosting | 72.8 | 95.5 | 0.895 |
| noise floor | 67.9 | 88.8 | 0.909 |

The noise floor is a model that predicts the simulator's signal exactly and is wrong only by the injected noise: no model can beat it. Gradient boosting closes **84%** of the gap between the linear baseline and that floor. The remaining gap is the honest measure of what the model has not learned.

## 2. Prediction intervals

| | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Nominal | 80% |
| Raw quantile models | 71.2% |
| After split-conformal calibration | 79.9% |

Conformal margin 20 kg; mean calibrated interval width 240 kg. Raw quantile models under-cover on a later time window, which is exactly why the interval is calibrated on held-out data before it is allowed to gate decisions.

## 5. Counterfactual attribution vs ground truth

Controllable excess is estimated as *f(x) − f(x at benchmark operations)* and split across levers with exact Shapley values. Because the simulator's true split is known, the estimate can be scored:

| Check | Value |
|---|---|
| Correlation with true controllable kg | 0.973 |
| MAE of controllable estimate | 32 kg |
| True controllable share of excess | 35.3% |
| Estimated controllable share | 31.9% (-3.3 pp) |
| Dominant lever identified correctly | 85.4% |

| Lever | True mean (kg) | Estimated mean (kg) | Correlation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Taxi-out / ground congestion | 63.84 | 62.32 | 0.98 |
| Departure delay | 36.15 | 36.42 | 0.91 |
| Cruise-speed profile | 70.01 | 56.20 | 0.98 |
| APU usage / ground power | 35.40 | 33.90 | 0.97 |
| Route efficiency | 55.90 | 47.80 | 0.96 |

The estimate is systematically **conservative**: tree ensembles extrapolate flatly at the benchmark edge of the training distribution, so the counterfactual under-states the controllable component by a few points. The direction and size of that bias are known here; in production they would not be, which is the argument for validating attribution on a designed pilot rather than trusting it.

## 6. Decision policy — same review capacity, different lists

Top 10% of the held-out window (600 flights) under four ranking policies:

| Ranking policy | Capture of controllable fuel | Precision (actionable) | Mean true controllable (kg) | Contextual share of reviewed excess |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| oracle true controllable | 22.8% | 100.0% | 596 | 49.4% |
| controllable attribution | 22.4% | 100.0% | 585 | 49.3% |
| naive total predicted | 20.2% | 84.3% | 527 | 58.2% |
| random | 9.8% | 62.5% | 256 | 65.1% |

Ranking on the total prediction — the obvious policy — sends operators to flights whose excess is mostly weather, payload and sector length. Ranking on attributed controllable excess reaches **98%** of the oracle's capture with **100%** actionable precision.

Queue status on the window — no_action: 4,401, queued: 1,495, no_action_contextual: 88, review_low_confidence: 16. Abstention rate 0.3% (in-distribution data; abstention exists for the day the data is not). Dominant levers in the queue: Cruise-speed profile 50%, Taxi-out / ground congestion 32%, APU usage / ground power 10%, Route efficiency 8%, Departure delay 0%.

## 7. Drift monitoring — three windows, three signatures

Reference = season-matched training flights. Thresholds: PSI ≥ 0.1 WATCH, ≥ 0.2 REVIEW; residual shift |z| ≥ 3 REVIEW.

**Held-out window, unmodified**

All monitors OK.

*max feature PSI 0.059; residual shift z = -0.0*

**Scenario A — measurement drift (+20% recorded taxi-out, fuel unchanged)**

| monitor | name | statistic | value | flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| feature | taxi_out_min | psi | 0.151 | WATCH |
| concept | mean_residual_kg | z | -17.264 | REVIEW |

*max feature PSI 0.151; residual shift z = -17.3*

**Scenario B — operational drift (airspace constraint, route efficiency −0.08, fuel recomputed)**

| monitor | name | statistic | value | flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| feature | route_efficiency_score | psi | 8.973 | REVIEW |

*max feature PSI 8.973; residual shift z = +2.7*

Measurement drift (a data-feed definition change) barely registers on feature PSI and is caught by the residual monitor; operational drift (the world changed) is loud on feature PSI while residuals stay quiet because the model is still right. A monitoring design that only watches inputs would miss the first; one that only watches errors would be late on the second.

## 8. Value model (illustrative)

| Scenario | Prioritised share | Adoption | Realisation | Avg controllable (kg) | Fuel saved (kg / yr) | Net value (AED / yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Downside | 10% | 55% | 35% | 400 | 492,800 | -1,514,400 |
| Base | 10% | 70% | 50% | 500 | 1,575,000 | 1,437,500 |
| Upside | 10% | 80% | 60% | 600 | 3,168,000 | 7,004,000 |
| Base (pipeline-informed) | 10% | 70% | 50% | 585 | 1,842,750 | 2,106,875 |

The pipeline-informed row replaces guessed inputs with the queue the decision engine actually produced. Everything else — adoption, realisation, fuel price — is an operating assumption, and the spread between rows is the point: the model's contribution ends at "prioritised".

## How to read this page

* These are simulator results. They say nothing about any airline's fuel performance.
* The simulator is disclosed in full and the same code is used to validate the method; that is its purpose.
* The right questions for a real deployment are in `MODEL_CARD.md` §10 and `FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md`.
